Here is the fantasy the whole CS category is built on. That the CSM owns the renewal.

You don't.

The renewal is a procurement event. It's decided by whether your exec champion still has budget and still has a job. It's settled in a finance review you were never invited to, against a pricing model you did not set, in a quarter shaped by a reorg no health score predicted.

I've watched green-scored accounts crater on a single sponsor change. I've watched red-flagged ones save themselves because a new champion inherited a bigger budget.

So when Gainsight repositioned itself as retention-as-a-service, telling the market it will own the renewal motion end to end, boards leaned in. Not because they discovered something new. Because CS never made its human labor legible. The board had no way to tell the difference between a renewal a machine can run and one it can't.

The renewal is not yours to own.

But the change order is. And you gave it away for free.

She counted them off a note she'd started keeping in Apple Notes. Her manager kept asking why she looked exhausted going into renewals.

The custom Salesforce dashboard a VP wanted before a board meeting.

The ad-hoc training for a team that never showed up to the paid one.

The integration triage when the customer's own engineer broke the webhook.

The exec deck she built from a blank slide at 9pm because the sponsor had a QBR the next morning.

Every one of those got called "the relationship."

In professional services, every one of those is a priced change order. A documented variation. A line item someone signs.

CS imported the "do whatever it takes" ethos from professional services. And left behind the one discipline that ever made that ethos survivable.

Unpriced generosity is not a relationship strategy. It's an unfunded liability with a smiling face.

How many out-of-contract favors did you absorb last quarter? Have you ever actually counted?

Here's how to fix it. The Scope Line framework.

1. Start a favor ledger.
Log every request that falls outside the contract for one full quarter. Total the hours per account. You cannot manage what you have never once counted.

2. Draw the Scope Line.
Separate what the renewal actually pays for from the favor load you silently absorb.

3. Route everything outside the line.
Send it to product, to priced services, or to a documented no. Not the same reflexive yes.

4. Keep the handful a machine can never fake.
The boardroom moment. The political read. The trust that survives a sponsor change. That's your defensible core.

Professional services firms figured this out decades ago. Not because they were cold. Because they intended to still be in business next quarter.

Generosity is real and it matters. But generosity without a change order looks a lot like something a board could buy cheaper.

For years I believed the unpriced extra was what separated a great CSM from an average one. The 9pm deck. The dashboard nobody paid for. The training session that wasn't in scope.

I wore the exhaustion like a badge.

Then I watched what happened when boards started asking a colder question. Not "is this CSM generous?" but "could a machine do this cheaper?"

And I realized the generosity I was proudest of was the exact thing making my role economically indefensible. I had spent years making myself easy to replace, and calling it relationship building.

The hard truth I had to sit with is this. Generosity without a change order isn't loyalty. It's an unfunded liability. And boards have started noticing.

The fix isn't to stop being generous. It's to count it. Route what isn't yours to carry. Keep the handful a machine will never fake.

The renewal was never yours to own. But the line that decides whether a human was necessary at all still is. For now.
